subject: Greece
note: Cited to one pinned Wikipedia revision (trusted_secondary): Corinth Canal. The page gives the length twice, 6.4 km in the lead and 6,343 m under Layout; a script uses 6.4 km. The page says completed in 1893 but formally opened in July 1893 and not open to navigation until November 1894, so a script says only 'completed in 1893'. The 24.6 m is the width at the surface and is also the page's stated maximum ship width. The map marks only the page's infobox coordinate (approximate) and draws no route round the Peloponnese: the page gives the 700 km as a figure and no geometry. Natural Earth has no outline for the gulfs here.

claims.text: The Corinth Canal connects the Gulf of Corinth with the Saronic Gulf; completed in 1893, it cuts through the narrow Isthmus of Corinth and separates the Peloponnese peninsula from the Greek mainland.
The canal was dug through the Isthmus at sea level and has no locks.
It is 6.4 kilometres (4 miles) in length and 24.6 metres wide at sea level.
The rock walls rise 90 metres (300 ft) above sea level, at a near-vertical 80° angle.
The canal saves a 700-kilometre (430 mi) journey around the Peloponnese for transiting vessels.
It is too narrow and shallow for large, deep-drafted oceangoing vessels, accommodating a maximum of 24.6 metres (81 ft) in width and 7.3 metres (24 ft) in draft.

The emperor Nero was the first to attempt to construct the canal, breaking the ground with a pickaxe in 67 AD, but the project was abandoned when he died shortly afterwards; the modern canal follows the same course as Nero's.
The tyrant Periander proposed it in the 7th century BC but instead built the Diolkos, a land trackway along which ships could be towed.
The canal is currently used mainly by tourist ships; around 15,000 ships per year (an average of about 40 per day) travel through the waterway.
The canal closed at the beginning of 2021 after a landslide and reopened on 1 June 2023.
